lessons.body:
Testing Strategy and Confidence
Pyramid
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Testing is risk management, not line counting
Test the boundary you are trying to prove

Pure rule                Service              Repository             HTTP API             Browser

no framework               fake repo           real Postgres           Nest + DB           real UI flow

Do not start a database to prove a pure status transition.

Do not mock Prisma when the thing you need to prove is your Prisma query.

A good suite puts many fast tests around business rules, fewer real-database/API tests around
integration boundaries, and a small number of expensive browser tests around revenue/security/critical
workflows.

TaskFlow layers
• Pure unit: status transition matrix, due-date policy, query normalization, path builders.

• Service: TasksService orchestration with fake TaskRepository.

• Repository integration: Prisma query shapes, tenant scoping, pagination, constraints.

• HTTP/e2e: Nest pipeline, Zod validation, guards, filters, serialization, real DB.

• Component/integration: form behavior, accessible errors, query mutation UX.

• Browser E2E: sign in -> open workspace -> create/update Task -> persisted result.

Anti-patterns
• A giant E2E suite for every edge case: slow and brittle.

• Mocking every dependency until the test proves only the mock setup.

• Repository unit tests with mocked Prisma when the SQL/query semantics are the thing under test.

• Snapshot tests as the primary way to prove application behavior.

• Coverage percentage treated as proof of correctness.

lessons.body:
Vitest Monorepo Setup and Test
Commands
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Why Vitest now
NestJS 12 newly generated projects use Vitest by default, while Next.js provides an official Vitest setup
guide. Using one primary runner reduces cognitive overhead without forcing browser E2E into the same
tool.

Install plan
# API
pnpm --filter api add -D vitest@5.0.1 @nestjs/testing@12.0.3 supertest@7.2.2

# Web
pnpm --filter web add -D vitest@5.0.1 jsdom@30.1.0 \
@testing-library/react@16.3.3 @testing-library/dom@10.4.2 \
@testing-library/jest-dom@7.0.1 @testing-library/user-event@14.6.7

# Browser E2E at workspace root
pnpm add -Dw @playwright/test@1.63.0
pnpm exec playwright install

Scripts
{
"scripts": {
"test": "turbo run test",
"test:unit": "turbo run test:unit",
"test:integration": "turbo run test:integration",
"test:e2e": "playwright test"
}
}

Naming conventions
• *.spec.ts - unit/service tests colocated with code.

• *.integration.spec.ts - tests that require a real external dependency such as PostgreSQL.

• *.e2e-spec.ts - Nest application HTTP tests.

• e2e/*.spec.ts - Playwright browser journeys.

lessons.body:
Prisma Repository Integration Tests
with PostgreSQL
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Why this layer must be real
A Prisma repository exists specifically to encode persistence behavior. Its important risks are relation
filters, tenant scoping, count queries, sort order, constraints and PostgreSQL behavior. Mocking Prisma
cannot prove those things.

Dedicated test database lifecycle
1. create/reset dedicated TEST_DATABASE_URL
2. prisma migrate deploy
3. seed minimal scenario data
4. run repository integration tests
5. cleanup/reset
6. never point this command at development or production

Scoped query example
• Seed Workspace A + User A membership + Task A.

• Seed Workspace B + Task B with no membership for User A.

• Call listScoped(userA).

• Assert Task A is returned and Task B never appears.

• Repeat with filtering/pagination/count so security scope and collection metadata are proven together.

Isolation strategy
Start simple: transaction/reset or ordered deleteMany cleanup against a dedicated database. Parallelize
integration tests only after data isolation is designed explicitly; speed is not worth cross-test
contamination.

lessons.body:
NestJS HTTP E2E: Authentication and
Authorization
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

What the HTTP suite proves
This layer exercises the assembled Nest request path: CORS-independent HTTP handling, validation
pipes, AuthGuard, permission checks, controllers, exception filter, repository and PostgreSQL.

Boot the real application module
const moduleRef = await Test.createTestingModule({
imports: [AppModule],
})
.overrideProvider(SupabaseAuthService)
.useValue(testAuthVerifier)
.compile()

app = moduleRef.createNestApplication(
new FastifyAdapter(),
)

await configureApp(app)
await app.init()
await app.getHttpAdapter().getInstance().ready()

Security matrix
• No token -> 401.

• Malformed/unknown token -> 401.

• Authenticated TaskFlow user with no membership -> scoped 404/403 according to contract.

• Workspace MEMBER can update assigned Task but cannot delete.

• ADMIN can perform allowed elevated operations.

• Changing Task ID to a different Workspace never bypasses scoping.

• Invalid body still returns Phase 12 validation envelope.

• Unexpected failure still returns Phase 13 safe 500 envelope with requestId.

Test auth without testing Supabase itself
The HTTP suite may override the external token verifier with deterministic token-to-claims
fixtures. That keeps focus on TaskFlow guards and authorization. A smaller separate
smoke/integration check can verify the real Supabase environment when needed.

lessons.body:
React Component and Form Testing
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Test through user-visible behavior
React Testing Library encourages tests that resemble how users find and operate the UI. Prefer
accessible roles/labels over CSS selectors, component internals, or implementation-specific state.

Form example
const user = userEvent.setup()
render(<TaskForm mode="create" projectId={PROJECT_ID} />)

await user.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: /create task/i }))

expect(
await screen.findByText(/title is required/i),
).toBeVisible()

await user.type(
screen.getByRole("textbox", { name: /title/i }),
"Prepare payroll",
)

High-value component behaviors
• Accessible label/error association.

• Blank title blocks submission.

• Pending mutation disables duplicate submit.

• 403/409 keeps user-entered values.

• Edit mode starts clean and becomes dirty after change.

• Permission-aware UI does not show an unavailable action - while API tests separately prove security.

Async Server Components
Next.js currently recommends E2E coverage rather than relying on Vitest for async Server Components.
Keep unit/component tests around synchronous Client Components and extracted logic, then prove
async route composition through Playwright.

lessons.summary: TanStack Query Testing and Cache Isolation TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026 Never share a QueryClient across tests function createTestQueryClient() { return new QueryClient({ defaultOptions: { queries: { retry: false }, mutations: { retry: false }, }, }) } Why retries are disabled in tests…
lessons.body:
TanStack Query Testing and Cache
Isolation
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Never share a QueryClient across tests
function createTestQueryClient() {
return new QueryClient({
defaultOptions: {
queries: { retry: false },
mutations: { retry: false },
},
})
}

Why retries are disabled in tests
Application retry behavior has dedicated tests. Disabling default retry loops makes ordinary failure tests
deterministic and prevents “expected error” tests from waiting through backoff.

Optimistic update scenarios from Phase 25
• Prediction appears immediately.

• Server success reconciles with authoritative Task.

• 403/409 restores rollback snapshot.

• Old in-flight query cannot overwrite the optimistic cache after cancellation.

• Same-Task serialized mutations preserve ordering.

• Query invalidation happens at the intended key scope.

Network boundary
Mock the HTTP API boundary for component/query tests rather than mocking TanStack Query itself. The
thing under test is how TaskFlow uses Query behavior, not whether TanStack Query can cache data.

Workflows

Critical TaskFlow user journey

Browser                Next.js                 NestJS                   Prisma          Postgres

Playwright critical-path test
one test can prove the wiring across the stack

Browser tests are expensive but high-confidence. Reserve them for workflows where broken wiring,
navigation, authentication, JavaScript behavior or browser semantics would hurt users materially.

Recommended TaskFlow journey
• Start with a known test account/session fixture.

• Open authorized Workspace Tasks.

• Create a Task through the real form.

• Observe it in the list.

• Change status and confirm UI converges.

• Reload the page and confirm persistence.

• Attempt one forbidden action with a lower-privilege user.

Locator rule
await page.getByRole("button", {
name: "Create task",
}).click()

await page.getByLabel("Title")
.fill("Prepare payroll")

await expect(
page.getByText("Prepare payroll"),
).toBeVisible()

Production-like execution
Next.js recommends running Playwright against a built/running app for production-like behavior.
Playwright gives each test an isolated browser context and supports Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.

lessons.body:
Fixtures, Factories, Determinism and
Isolation
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

A test fixture is a scenario, not a dump of production
data
Build the smallest domain graph that explains the test: one user, one Workspace membership, one
Project, one Task. Large global fixtures make failures harder to understand.

Factory example
export function task(overrides: Partial<TaskRecord> = {}): TaskRecord {
return {
id: "00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
projectId: PROJECT_ID,
assigneeId: USER_ID,
title: "Test task",
status: "TODO",
priority: "MEDIUM",
completedAt: null,
createdAt: FIXED_TIME,
updatedAt: FIXED_TIME,
...overrides,
}
}

Sources of flakiness to control
• Current time and timezone.

• Random UUIDs when identity matters to assertions.

• Shared database rows across parallel tests.

• Retries and background refetches.

• Unawaited async work.

• Network calls to external providers.

• Order-dependent tests.

Test independence
A test should pass by itself, after any other test, and in a shuffled order. If it requires “test
3” to run first, the suite is describing a script rather than independent evidence.

lessons.body:
Coverage, Test Quality and CI
Readiness
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Coverage is a signal, not a target game
• High line coverage can still miss authorization mistakes, bad assertions and incorrect requirements.

• Prefer coverage around business branches and security decisions, not trivial getters.

• Use uncovered lines to ask “is there meaningful behavior here?” rather than blindly chasing 100%.

Suggested gates before CI phase
pnpm lint
pnpm typecheck
pnpm test:unit
pnpm test:integration
pnpm build
pnpm test:e2e

Failure diagnostics
• Unit failure: show expected/actual values and focused stack trace.

• Repository integration: log scenario IDs and keep DB reset commands explicit.

• HTTP test: print response body on mismatch, never tokens/secrets.

• Playwright: retain trace/screenshot/video on retry/failure, not every passing run.

Do not make slow tests the local default
Developers need a fast inner loop. Unit/component tests should run constantly; repository/API/browser
suites can run explicitly or at pre-push/CI boundaries depending on cost.

lessons.body:
Hands-On Lab and Phase Exit
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Lab 1 - Pure policy
• Write table-driven tests for every allowed and rejected Task status transition.

• Add one deterministic due-date policy test with a fixed clock input.

Lab 2 - Service
• Use FakeTaskRepository.

• Prove MEMBER can update an assigned Task.

• Prove a denied transition produces the expected application exception.

Lab 3 - Repository + PostgreSQL
• Create two Workspaces and two Tasks.

• Prove listScoped never leaks the unrelated Workspace.

• Prove pagination totalItems is computed inside the same authorization filter.

Lab 4 - HTTP security
• 401 without identity.

• 403 or scoped 404 for unauthorized resource/action.

• 400 for invalid DTO.

• 200/201 for valid authorized request.

Lab 5 - Frontend
• Form error can be found by accessible text/role.

• TanStack optimistic failure rolls back.

• No shared QueryClient state leaks between tests.

Lab 6 - Browser
• Playwright: sign in fixture -> create Task -> update status -> reload -> persisted state.

• Repeat one permission-denied workflow with MEMBER role.

Phase exit checklist
• I can explain unit vs integration vs HTTP/e2e vs browser E2E.

• I know when a fake repository is appropriate and when a real database is required.

• I can test authentication/authorization without trusting the browser.

• I can test a React form through accessible interactions rather than internals.

• I can keep TanStack Query tests isolated.

• I can design one critical Playwright journey instead of browser-testing every edge case.

• I understand that coverage is evidence, not correctness.

lessons.body:
Guided Build Lab — Phase 28: Testing

Purpose
Build a testing strategy that proves pure rules, service orchestration, repositories, HTTP contracts, frontend behavior, and critical browser flows at the right cost.

Deliverable
Vitest + integration + Playwright test suite with deterministic fixtures and CI-ready commands.

Before you touch the code
Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything.

Architecture trace
risk/question -> choose boundary -> arrange controlled state -> execute behavior -> assert outcome/contract -> cleanup

Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization.

Step 1 — List the highest-risk TaskFlow behaviors before choosing test counts.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 2 — Write a pure unit test for one deterministic business policy.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 3 — Test a service with controlled dependencies and assert business outcome rather than private calls.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 4 — Run a repository integration test against real PostgreSQL with isolated data.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 5 — Run an API test through NestJS for validation/auth/error contract.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 6 — Write one Playwright flow for a critical user journey and make setup/cleanup reproducible.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Useful verification commands
pnpm test
pnpm --filter api test
pnpm --filter web test
pnpm exec playwright test

Do not run commands mechanically. Before each command, predict what successful output should prove. If it fails, capture the exact message and identify whether the failure is environment, dependency, compile-time, runtime, network, authorization, or persistence related.

Checkpoint
When the lab works, inspect git diff. Remove accidental debugging output and unrelated edits. Run type checking/tests/build commands relevant to this phase. Commit the checkpoint with a message that describes the capability added, not merely the files changed.

Explain-back
Without looking at the lesson, explain why each layer in the architecture trace exists, what this phase added to TaskFlow, and what would break if the new responsibility were moved to the wrong layer. If you cannot explain the boundary, repeat the trace before moving on.

lessons.title: Debugging Workshop
lessons.summary:
Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.
lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 28: Testing

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
risk/question -> choose boundary -> arrange controlled state -> execute behavior -> assert outcome/contract -> cleanup

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Mocking the thing the test is supposed to prove
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Huge number of brittle snapshot/UI implementation tests
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Shared mutable test data causing order-dependent failures
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — E2E used for every rule, making feedback too slow
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Testing

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 28 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Build a testing strategy that proves pure rules, service orchestration, repositories, HTTP contracts, frontend behavior, and critical browser flows at the right cost.

Required artifact
Vitest + integration + Playwright test suite with deterministic fixtures and CI-ready commands.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can choose test level by risk.
• Can write deterministic tests.
• Can test real persistence when needed.
• Can explain what each test does not prove.

Independent build sequence
1. List the highest-risk TaskFlow behaviors before choosing test counts.
2. Write a pure unit test for one deterministic business policy.
3. Test a service with controlled dependencies and assert business outcome rather than private calls.
4. Run a repository integration test against real PostgreSQL with isolated data.
5. Run an API test through NestJS for validation/auth/error contract.
6. Write one Playwright flow for a critical user journey and make setup/cleanup reproducible.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

lessons.body:
Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 28: Testing. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
Vitest + integration + Playwright test suite with deterministic fixtures and CI-ready commands.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

objectives: Build a testing strategy that proves pure rules, service orchestration, repositories, HTTP contracts, frontend behavior, and critical browser flows at the right cost.
Produce a reproducible evidence packet for success and failure.
Defend the architecture and identify one improvement without overengineering.

references.preview:
# TaskFlow Phase 28 Testing Snapshot

This snapshot demonstrates the intended testing boundaries. It is reference code, not a wholesale replacement for every existing file.

Test layers:
1. Pure unit policies
2. Nest service tests with fake repositories
3. Prisma repository integration tests with a dedicated PostgreSQL database
4. Nest HTTP e2e tests
5. React/TanStack component tests
6. Playwright critical browser journeys

- NestJS Testing: https://docs.nestjs.com/fundamentals/testing
- Prisma ORM v7 Testing: https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/more/best-practices
- Prisma Unit Testing: https://docs.prisma.io/docs/orm/prisma-client/testing/unit-testing
- Next.js Vitest: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/testing/vitest
- Next.js Playwright: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/testing/playwright
- React Testing Library: https://testing-library.com/docs/react-testing-library/intro/
- TanStack Query Testing: https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/testing
- Playwright: https://playwright.dev/docs/browsers
- Vitest npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/vitest
- React Testing Library npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@testing-library/react
- Playwright npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@playwright/test

# Testing strategy

- Pure rules: no framework, no database.
- TasksService: FakeTaskRepository.
- PrismaTaskRepository: real PostgreSQL.
- API security/contracts: boot Nest application, use Supertest.
- React components/forms: Vitest + Testing Library + jsdom.
- Query behavior: isolated QueryClient per test.
- Critical user journeys: Playwright.

Do not mock the dependency whose real behavior is the subject of the test.

# Phase 28 test matrix

## Unit
- allowed/rejected status transitions
- due-date policy with fixed time

## Service
- completedAt derived correctly
- business conflicts become domain exceptions

## Repository integration
- tenant scope never leaks rows
- filters/count/pagination share authorization scope

## HTTP
- 400 validation
- 401 unauthenticated
- 403/404 authorization semantics
- 409 business conflict
- safe 500 error contract
